analysis.one_liner: Makes opioid companies pay civil penalties, fees, and lost exclusivity for false marketing and oversupplying communities.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2019 by Senator Sanders with three Democratic cosponsors, the bill sat in the Senate health committee for the rest of the two-year Congress and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for opioid manufacturers and distributors to falsely advertise that opioids are not addictive, to ship more pills to a community than doctors there could reasonably use, or to sit on suspicious distribution orders. Companies caught doing it would owe 75 percent of their opioid profits, executives would lose salary and stock gains from the period, and offenders would lose market exclusivity. Every company that sold federally covered opioids since 1993 would pay a share of a $20 billion fee, and the money would fund treatment, prevention, family support, and school programs for communities hit by the epidemic.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities and families affected by the opioid epidemic, who would get the $20 billion fund for treatment, prevention, Head Start and school-based mental health programs; and pain patients, who would benefit from guardrails on reckless oversupply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families and communities hit by opioids

how_it_helps.text: Penalizes companies and their executives for three practices: falsely claiming opioids are not addictive, supplying communities with more opioids than are medically reasonable, and failing to report suspicious distribution orders.

Imposes a $20 billion fee on every company that made or distributed a federally covered opioid between 1993 and enactment, and directs the money to an Opioids Reimbursement Fund for treatment, family support, school prevention, and Head Start programs in hard-hit states.
Revokes market exclusivity for opioid makers found in violation and blocks 'product hopping' — reformulating a drug to win a new monopoly — which would speed cheaper generic competition.
Makes individual executives personally liable, with penalties equal to their salary plus any stock gains during the period of misconduct, and up to 10 years in prison for the worst violations.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers and distributors, which face civil penalties of up to 75 percent of their opioid profits, a share of the $20 billion fee, and lost market exclusivity; and their executives, who face personal pay-and-stock clawbacks and possible prison time.

drawbacks.text: The $20 billion fee applies to every company that sold a federally covered opioid since 1993, regardless of fault, so companies with modest or historic roles in the market pay the same kind of assessment as the major offenders.

Penalties are retroactive: they reach profits, salaries, and unsold stock gains from conduct that occurred before the law existed, which companies and legal scholars would likely challenge as beyond fair notice and which could take years of litigation to collect.

A blanket prohibition on supplying quantities that 'are not medically reasonable' creates uncertainty for pharmacists, wholesalers, and pain patients who depend on opioids, since the Secretary would have to build a formula for what counts as reasonable and honest prescribing could get caught up in enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is strong on its face: the opioid epidemic killed hundreds of thousands of Americans and the companies that marketed and oversupplied opioids largely escaped federal penalties, while this bill would claw back money from the companies and executives and put it into treatment and prevention. The honest counterweights are the retroactive, near-automatic fee on every company that ever touched the market, and the legal fragility of penalties that reach back to unsold stock gains. Those design problems are real but addressable; the larger cost to the public was that the bill never moved at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the Opioid Crisis Accountability Act of 2019 on May 21, 2019, for himself along with Senators Bennet, Harris, and Blumenthal.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Three Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the record for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers and distributors, who never faced the $20 billion assessment, the profit-based civil penalties, executive pay clawbacks, or loss of market exclusivity the bill would have imposed — and the communities hit by the epidemic got none of the $20 billion for treatment and prevention.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its penalty, fee, and reimbursement-fund provisions.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats or an independent; the three cosponsors were all Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Senate committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would impose civil penalties worth 75 percent of their opioid profits, strip market exclusivity, and expose executives to pay-and-stock clawbacks and prison. For ordinary people, that money and the $20 billion fund are what the industry would pay for its role in the epidemic.

Distributors would face penalties for shipping medically unreasonable quantities to communities and for failing to report suspicious order patterns, plus a share of the $20 billion fee. Those oversupply and silence duties are precisely the conduct blamed for flooding towns with pills.

industries.industry: Generic drug makers and holders of opioid market exclusivity
industries.note: Companies found in violation would lose exclusivity, letting cheaper generics in, but any drugmaker that ever sold a covered opioid since 1993 owes part of the $20 billion fee even without a violation. Consumers benefit from faster generic competition; the fee reaches some firms with little connection to the epidemic.
